lesson_title: The Queue That Explains Every Sound You Hear
hook_text: Someone bumps the back of the taxi queue — and accidentally demonstrates how every sound reaches your ear.
clip_script: Friday afternoon at the rank, and the queue for the last taxi is long. Somebody at the back loses their balance and bumps the person ahead. That person lurches into the next, who nudges the next — and a squash of people travels the whole queue to the front. But watch: nobody walked up the line. Everyone rocked forward and stepped back into their own spot. Only the squash made the journey. Now swap every person for an air molecule, and you are not imagining any more — you are hearing. A speaker cone pushes forward and squashes the air; pulls back and leaves a gap. Squash, gap, squash, gap, streaming across the room until one squash lands on your eardrum. That press is sound. It is why space is silent — no particles, nothing to squash — and why sound rips through steel at five thousand metres a second but only manages three hundred and forty through air: tight queues pass the message faster. How often the squashes arrive is pitch. How hard they arrive is loudness. One bumped queue, and the whole physics of sound falls out of it.
visual_style: A stylised queue of glowing figures with a bright squash pulsing forward through them; morph the figures into air molecules streaming toward a giant ear; speed race between a steel beam, a water column and open air; labels stamp in for pitch and loudness.
mood: A street scene that quietly turns into a physics lecture.
pacing: Playful build through the queue bump, smooth morph into molecules, quick-fire speed comparison, tight two-label recap.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never mix up pitch and loudness again.
